<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-salt" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-salt-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of salt, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>36</td><td>20%</td></tr><tr><td>Caridi et al. 2019</td><td>2</td><td>20%</td></tr><tr><td>Fayet-Moore et al. 2020</td><td>29</td><td>20%</td></tr><tr><td>Stojanović et al. 2021</td><td>2</td><td>20%</td></tr><tr><td>Wu et al. 2021</td><td>1</td><td>20%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for salt, as sold on a as sold, as eaten or fresh weight basis: monitoring results summarized as one median per reporting region, sampling type and collection year, total diet composites and printed sample values as single observations, and printed subgroup medians from ordinary farms or markets. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>5 sampling families with different designs; none is a probability sample of world supply. Reporting regions and purchase markets are not growing areas. Non-detects with differing limits widen the bounds. Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, salt, as sold had the lowest lead subgroup median in AFRO (57 µg/kg) and the highest in PAHO (156 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For cadmium, the lowest regional median was in AFRO (1 µg/kg) and the highest in EMRO (7.7 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

In one study, lead across 29 groups of salt ranged from 30 µg/kg (pink salt retail product 10) to 2,590 µg/kg (pink salt retail product 17); the lowest is the lowest observed in that study, not an established sourcing preference.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fayetmoore2020-australia-pink-salt-minerals|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Fayet-Moore F, Wibisono C, Carr P, Duve E, Petocz P, Lancaster G, McMillan J, Marshall S, Blumfield M · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fayetmoore2020-australia-pink-salt-minerals">An Analysis of the Mineral Composition of Pink Salt Available in Australia</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Foods 2020, 9(10), 1490</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fayetmoore2020-australia-pink-salt-minerals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In another study, lead across 6 groups of salt ranged from 5,240 µg/kg (gourmet salt) to 9,240 µg/kg (gourmet salt, origin Iran, bought in Messina markets); the lowest is the lowest observed in that study, not an established sourcing preference.<sup class="cite">[[sources/disalvo2023-gourmet-table-salts-minerals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Di Salvo E, Tardugno R, Nava V, Naccari C, Virga A, Salvo A, Corbo F, Clodoveo ML, Cicero N · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/disalvo2023-gourmet-table-salts-minerals">Gourmet Table Salts: The Mineral Composition Showdown</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxics 2023, 11, 705</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/disalvo2023-gourmet-table-salts-minerals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>
